title: How to Evaluate Text-to-SQL on Your Own Database
summary: A runnable method for getting a text-to-SQL accuracy number that applies to your warehouse: building the question set, fixing the grading rule first, repeating runs, and counting refusals apart from errors.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Evaluate a text-to-SQL system with questions representative of your database and business definitions. Report correct answers, refusals and wrong answers separately, then inspect latency, cost and access-control behaviour under a fixed configuration.**


You get a number that means something by writing the questions yourself, fixing the grading rule before you look at any results, running the whole set at least three times, and declaring both accuracy denominators, one over answered questions and one over the whole answerable set, so refusing more cannot look like improving. Four decisions, none of them about the model.


The grading rule alone moves the answer. Beacon, the open grader behind our published comparison, records a re-basing: Spider EX on one local slice read 53.4% under the runner's own grading and 55.7% under beacon's, on the same run. Nothing was rerun. Two definitions of "correct" met the same rows.


The usual version of "evaluate on your own data" is a demo on a dozen questions somebody made up in a meeting. That tells you the system can write SQL. It cannot tell you how often it will be wrong, and it has no error bar, because twelve questions cannot carry one.


We're not claiming you need a thousand questions before you learn anything. Twenty to thirty, tagged by difficulty band, will tell you which layer to fix. It just won't tell you whether 61% beats 58%.


Start with the question set, not the tooling. Pull real questions out of your BI tool's query log, write a reference answer for each, tag each one as answerable from column names, needs a definition, or should be refused, and keep right, refused and wrong as three separate numbers.


## Overview


Someone has asked you to say whether a text-to-SQL system is good enough for your warehouse. The vendor has a deck with a BIRD score on it. You know, or suspect, that the score is not about your database.


That suspicion is correct and we've argued it separately:[why BIRD and Spider rankings disagree](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/blog/why-bird-and-spider-rankings-disagree) takes apart the public corpora and the ordering flips between them. This is the other half, and it is the useful half. Assume no leaderboard transfers. What do you run to get a number about your own schema, and what has to be true of that number before you quote it?


The parts that decide the answer are boring and mostly not the model: the question set, the reference answers, the grading rule, the number of runs, and what happens to a question the system declines. Get those wrong and you still get a percentage. It just isn't a measurement of the thing you care about. Governance controls are a separate subject, covered in[mnemiq and governed data agents](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/blog/mnemiq/governed-data-agents) ; this is the measurement procedure, and it assumes you know which schema slice you may point at.


**Figure 1 — The evaluation loop, with every decision point named. The two gates that get skipped are stratification and writing the grading rule down first, and skipping either makes the loop's output uninterpretable.**


**The rule we'd start from:** choose the grading rule before you see any output. Any rule chosen afterwards is a rule chosen because of what it scored, and that is tuning, not grading.


## Where the Questions Come From, and How Many


Questions you invent at a whiteboard are biased toward the schema you remember. Real questions are biased toward what people need, which is the bias you want.


Three sources carry them. Your BI tool's query log is the richest: Looker, Tableau and Metabase all retain executed queries, and a quarter's worth tells you which tables carry traffic and which joins analysts actually write. The analytics team's backlog is second, and better in one respect, because a backlog item is a question nobody has answered yet. Third, support and internal-helpdesk tickets, where the phrasing is unpolished in the way a real user's phrasing is unpolished. "how many enterprise accounts churned last quarter" is a harder and more honest input than "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts WHERE ...".


Then stratify, because uniform sampling buries the result. Take a renewals analytics slice at a B2B software company: a third of the questions are single-table counts, a third need a join through a lookup table, and a handful turn on what "churned" means. Sample uniformly and the easy third dominates the percentage.


The bands we'd use, which are mnemiq's own tags in its README guidance, are *answerable from column names* , *needs a definition* , and *should be refused* . The diagnosis falls out of the comparison. Definition-band failures with schema-band passes mean a glossary problem, and writing one will pay for itself. Schema-band failures mean retrieval or enrichment. Both bands passing while the should-refuse band answers confidently means the system has no brakes.


Be honest about what each count buys. Twenty to thirty questions is a diagnostic: enough to say which band is broken, not enough to rank two configurations. Ranking needs real statistical power, and the numbers are larger than people expect. Evan Miller's paper on eval statistics works the arithmetic for a paired comparison and lands on roughly 969 questions to detect a three-point difference at 80% power and 5% significance. Two of its five recommendations bite hardest here: clustered standard errors when questions arrive in related groups, and inference on question-level paired differences rather than on two independent means. Clustering is unavoidable in this domain, because ten questions about the same fact table share its quirks and are not ten independent draws. Pretending otherwise makes your confidence interval too narrow and your improvements too convincing.


**A practical floor:** 25 questions to find out what to fix. Several hundred before you claim one configuration beats another. If you only have 25, say "the definition band fails" and not "we measured 64%".


## The Record Template, Field by Field


Everything in this method reduces to one table, in a spreadsheet, a CSV or a JSON file. Reuse it for every system and configuration, because a comparison is only valid if both sides were recorded in the same shape.


One row is **one question under one run** . Twenty-eight questions, three runs, two configurations is 168 rows, not 28, and that is the point: the per-run rows are what give you a spread and a flip rate. The first five fields belong to the question and never change; the last six are written by the run.


Field Written when Allowed values Why it is there


` question_id` authoring a stable string, e.g.` churn-q1` Joins one question across runs, configurations and systems. Renumbering it breaks every historical comparison silently.


` question` authoring the natural-language text, verbatim As a real user phrased it. Rewriting it into something the engine handles better is tuning the test.


` answerability` authoring` answerable-from-schema` ,` needs-definition` ,` should-refuse` The three bands. This field, not the accuracy column, tells you which layer to fix.


` required_definition` authoring the business term and its agreed meaning, or empty What "churned" or "last quarter" has to mean. If two people disagree here, the question is not gradeable yet.


` expected_result` authoring the reference **rows** , or` none` for` should-refuse` Rows, not gold SQL. Keep the gold SQL beside it as provenance; grade against the rows. On a` should-refuse` row the only passing outcome is` refused_correctly` .


` role` run the role or principal the question was asked as Access control is part of the measurement: the same question as` analyst` and as` support` should not return the same rows, and a system that ignores the role is wrong even when the number is right.


` system_version` run product and version, or` not disclosed` A figure without a version is not reproducible. Record non-disclosure rather than leaving it empty.


` configuration` run every setting that was varied, as one pinned descriptor Complete enough to rebuild the run from the cell. "The usual settings" is how a comparison stops being one.


` outcome` run` correct` ,` correct_facts` ,` wrong` ,` refused_correctly` ,` refused_wrongly` ,` error` Six values, not two: the vocabulary the denominators are built from.


` latency_ms` run wall-clock ms, question in to answer out Per row, so you can quote a median and a p95 rather than a mean that hides the tail. A configuration that wins on accuracy and triples latency may still lose.


` cost` run per-question cost, with the unit named Tokens, currency or both. Enrichment, multi-candidate generation and a verifier pass all buy accuracy with cost; omitting it compares different budgets.


A single row, written out:


json


```text
{
"question_id"  :   "churn-q1"  ,
"question"  :   "how many enterprise accounts churned last quarter?"  ,
"answerability"  :   "needs-definition"  ,
"required_definition"  :   "churned = churned_at is set; enterprise = segment_cd 'A' via segment lookup; last quarter = 2026-07-01..2026-09-30"  ,
"expected_result"  : [{   "n"  :   142   }],
"role"  :   "analyst"  ,
"system_version"  :   "mnemiq 0.1 (commit 9f2c1ab)"  ,
"configuration"  :   "model=<pinned model id and snapshot>, temperature=0, seed=7, embed=<model>, retrieval=k12, enrichment=tier2, certified_definitions=none, verifier=off, grader=beacon v7, schema_snapshot=2026-10-05"  ,
"outcome"  :   "correct"  ,
"latency_ms"  :   4120  ,
"cost"  :   "0.021 USD"
}
```


## The Denominators, Written Down Before You Run Anything


This is the part that decides whether the percentage can be gamed. A system can raise an accuracy figure two ways: by getting more questions right, or by declining the ones it would have got wrong. Only one of those is an improvement, and a single fraction cannot tell you which happened.


So fix the counts first. Over a set of` question_id` s, with` answerability` splitting them:


- **` answerable`** : every row whose` answerability` is` answerable-from-schema` or` needs-definition` . These have an` expected_result` .
- **` should_refuse`** : every row whose` answerability` is` should-refuse` . These are scored separately and never enter an accuracy fraction.
- **` errored`** : rows whose` outcome` is` error` , where nothing gradeable came back. An error is not a wrong answer and not a zero, so it leaves the answerable denominator, but it gets its own count: a system that errors on a fifth of your questions is unusable whatever its accuracy says.
- **` gradeable`** =` answerable` −` errored` . This is the denominator that matters.
- **` answered`** : gradeable rows whose` outcome` is` correct` ,` correct_facts` or` wrong` . Refusals are excluded here and only here.


And` errored` must not stay one bucket. "Twelve errors" is not a finding; these four have four different owners and four different fixes, so record a sub-reason beside the outcome:


Error class What it looks like Whose problem


Connection or permission the adapter could not reach the source, or the role was refused your deployment: credentials, network, grants. Not the model, and not a refusal either.


Invalid SQL the query did not compile or execute in the source dialect generation or dialect handling. A large count usually means the wrong dialect is being written: cheap to fix, easy to mistake for low accuracy.


Timeout or resource limit the statement was killed, or the result exceeded a cap the query, the warehouse or your limits. Record which limit fired; 5 s and 5 min are different results.


Model or harness failure the endpoint errored or rate-limited, returned nothing parseable, or the run crashed infrastructure. Retry these and say how many you retried: silently retrying until something works is how a flip rate disappears.


**Table 1 — Four error classes. A run with twenty connection errors and one with twenty invalid-SQL errors score identically and mean opposite things.**


Then report both of these, always as a pair:


Figure Numerator Denominator What it answers


Accuracy on attempts` correct` (or` correct` +` correct_facts` )` answered` When it does answer, how often is it right? Rises as the system refuses more.


Accuracy on the set` correct` (or` correct` +` correct_facts` )` gradeable` Of the questions a user could legitimately ask, how many came back with a right answer? Refusals count against it.


Deferral rate` refused_correctly` +` refused_wrongly`` gradeable` How much of your question set the system declines.


Over-refusal` refused_wrongly`` gradeable` Refusals a more permissive configuration answers correctly — the price of the caution.


Refusal hold` refused_correctly` on the should-refuse band` should_refuse` Whether the brakes work on questions where answering is the failure.


Error rate` errored`` answerable` How often nothing gradeable came back at all.


The pairing is the whole mechanism. **Accuracy on attempts** over **answered** is the figure most harnesses print, and a system that refuses half your questions and nails the rest scores beautifully on it. **Accuracy on the set** over **gradeable** keeps every refusal in the denominator, so that same system scores half as well. Quote them side by side and refusing more stops being a way to look better: it moves the first figure up and the second down, and the gap between them *is* the deferral rate. Run both under both grading rules and you have four numbers plus three rates, which is still fewer than the ways one percentage can mislead you.


**Declare the denominators in writing before the first run** , alongside the grading rule. A denominator chosen after you have seen the refusal count is the same mistake as a grading rule chosen after you have seen the rows.


## Reference Answers, and Deciding What Correct Means


A reference answer is not the gold SQL. It is the rows the gold SQL returns, and that is the artifact grading should compare against. **Grade the result of executing the query, never the text of the query.** Two queries that share no tokens can be equally correct: a join and a correlated subquery,` GROUP BY` against a window function, a` CTE` chain against one nested statement. String-matching marks all of those wrong, and equivalent SQL is not an edge case but the normal case. mnemiq's own harness is built that way: the README describes it as grading "results by the data returned rather than by string-matching the SQL", and in beacon the generated SQL is kept as evidence you can read, never as the thing that is scored.


Have a person who knows the data write the query, run it, and store the result. Then write down, before running anything, which of these rules decides whether a candidate matches. The[text-to-SQL evaluation taxonomy](https://agenticfabriq.github.io/text-to-sql-evaluation-taxonomy/#dimensions) calls this the grading rule dimension, and its four terms are the live options:


Rule Term id What it accepts


Exact result match` tsqlet:grading-rule/exact-result-match` The same columns as the reference, in the reference's order, no extras


Got the facts` tsqlet:grading-rule/got-the-facts` Every reference value present; extra columns and context are fine


LLM-judged` tsqlet:grading-rule/llm-judged` Whatever a model says satisfies the question


Human-judged` tsqlet:grading-rule/human-judged` Whatever a person accepts for the business question


Decide first because the same run scores differently under each. The taxonomy's[answer shape](https://github.com/agenticfabriq/text-to-sql-evaluation-taxonomy/blob/main/taxonomy/answer-shape.yaml) dimension names the band that moves:` tsqlet:answer-shape/right-data-wrong-shape` , defined as a result that "would pass got-the-facts but fail exact-result-match". An answer carrying` region, revenue, order_count` when the reference carries` region, revenue` is in that band. Exact match fails it. Got-the-facts passes it. Neither rule is wrong; they answer different questions, and an analyst who gets an extra column rarely files a bug.


**Figure 2 — One answer, three rules, three verdicts. The rule is not a detail of the measurement; on this band it is the measurement.**


Beacon's[grading contract](https://github.com/agenticfabriq/beacon/blob/main/docs/grading.md) shows how specific this has to get before it is reproducible. Got-the-facts there tolerates extra candidate columns, column order, row order, a decimal rounding either way under either convention, and the same value spelled differently. It refuses a missing gold column, a different row count, a different value, and` NULL` versus` 0` versus empty string. Whole numbers compare exactly under both readings, because "a count, a year, an id is right or wrong, never within a tolerance band." That is the detail a rule needs. "Correct" is not a rule.


And exact match isn't a safe default just because it is strict. The test-suite accuracy paper measured Spider's own exact-set-match metric against 21 leaderboard submissions and found a false-negative rate of 2.5% on average and 8.1% at worst, so a strict rule marks genuinely correct queries wrong often enough to reorder a leaderboard. Report both readings; the disagreement is information, not noise.


### Questions with more than one defensible reading


"How many payments did we take last quarter?" can mean distinct payment events or rows in the payments table, and where change-data-capture has left superseded revisions behind, those are different numbers. A question in that state is **not answerable yet** : leave it in and it grades as whatever reading the system happened to take that run, which turns your flip rate into noise. Pick one disposition before the first run.


1. **Pin the reading** in` required_definition` , store the rows for *that* reading in` expected_result` , and keep the row as` needs-definition` . Usually the right answer, and a test of whether your glossary exists: if nobody can say which reading is correct, the question has found a real gap.
2. **Split it** into two` question_id` s with two definitions and two reference results, when both readings are genuinely asked by different teams.
3. **Move it to` should-refuse`** , only if a clarification or a refusal is the behaviour you want. Then` expected_result` is` none` and the only passing outcome is` refused_correctly` .


What you must not do is score it as answerable and let the grader arbitrate. mnemiq takes the same line one level down, on values: coded values are grounded from the data, a standard code system or a hand-written dictionary with the source recorded, and are otherwise left bare, because "no evidence, no meaning". Where a column matches two code schemes ambiguously it writes a reviewable proposal instead of choosing silently. Ambiguity gets escalated rather than resolved by luck, and your question set should work the same way.


## Run It More Than Once


One run is not a measurement, and the reason is mechanical rather than philosophical. Stability is its own dimension in the taxonomy, with` tsqlet:stability/case-flip-rate` defined as the share of questions whose graded verdict changes across repeated identical runs, measured by running the full set at least three times with identical configuration and counting items not graded identically every time.


Temperature zero does not save you. Thinking Machines' write-up on inference nondeterminism sent 1,000 identical requests to Qwen3-235B at temperature 0 and got 80 unique completions, every one identical for the first 102 tokens and diverging at token 103. Their diagnosis is batch invariance rather than floating-point luck: "the primary reason nearly all LLM inference endpoints are nondeterministic is that the load (and thus batch-size) nondeterministically varies!" Your batch size is someone else's traffic.


Local servers add a second trap: they sample unless told not to. mnemiq's README records measuring this on vLLM 0.9, where Qwen2.5-Coder-32B ships temperature 0.7, a request naming no temperature gets the model's default, and five identical requests came back five different ways. Pinning temperature is necessary and not sufficient.


Report three things. The mean over runs rather than the best run, which the taxonomy calls` tsqlet:stability/mean-of-runs` . The spread between best and worst. And the case-flip rate, the number a stakeholder actually needs: the share of questions on which the system has no settled answer. A system at 64% mean with a 3% flip rate and one at 64% with an 18% flip rate are not the same product, and a single percentage cannot tell them apart.


Three runs is the floor. Resampling also reduces variance, so if a cell matters enough to argue about, run it more and say how many times.


### What goes in` system_version` and` configuration`


"Identical configuration" is only checkable if you wrote it down, which is what those two fields are for. A run is reproducible when a stranger could rebuild it from the two cells, as in theexample row :` system_version` takes the product plus a version, commit SHA or container digest, or the words *not disclosed* where a vendor gives none;` configuration` takes the model id **and** its snapshot, the endpoint, temperature and seed, the embedding model, retrieval depth, the enrichment tier and whether anyone certified a definition, the verifier threshold and whether verification is on at all, the grader and *its* version, and the schema snapshot the questions ran against. Changing the grader changes the metric, which is why it belongs beside the model rather than in a footnote.


Record whether the seed did anything, too. mnemiq forwards` MNEMIQ_LLM_SEED` to the provider and documents that vLLM honours it while the hosted endpoint accepts it and varies anyway, so a seed buys reproducibility on the local path only. "seed=7" without that caveat implies a determinism you do not have.


## Count Refusals Separately From Errors


A system that says "this schema has no revenue column" and one that returns a confident wrong number are not the same system, and one percentage cannot see the difference. Beacon states the two commitments plainly: "a deferral is not a failure. A system that declines to answer scores` DEFER` , not` FAIL` ", and "an error is not a zero. An attempt that never ran leaves the denominator instead of counting against the model."


Thedenominators are how you hold both of those at once. What the buckets cannot tell you on their own is whether the refusals were *earned* , and the taxonomy's[refusal](https://github.com/agenticfabriq/text-to-sql-evaluation-taxonomy/blob/main/taxonomy/refusal.yaml) dimension names the measurement that can:` tsqlet:refusal/calibrated-refusal` , the test of whether the questions a system declines are ones it would more often get wrong if forced.


It needs two configurations, so run the set with the verifier threshold high, then low. If the questions the strict configuration refused are ones the permissive configuration got wrong, the refusals earn their keep. If the permissive configuration answered them correctly, you are paying for caution in lost coverage, and the report should say so. The should-refuse band gives you the other half: deliberately unanswerable or unauthorized questions, where answering is the failure.


**One percentage is not a result.** Publish accuracy, deferral rate, over-refusal count, error count and case-flip rate together, or publish nothing. Any one of them can be improved by making another worse.


## Who or What Grades It


Three options, and each fails in a specific way.


**Result-set comparison** is the default and should be. It compares the rows your engine returned against the reference rows, under a rule you wrote down, and it is reproducible, cheap and auditable. It fails on questions whose answer is not a result set, and on reference errors: the taxonomy lists` tsqlet:failure-mode/reference-error` for a gold query that is itself wrong, which happens often enough that a strict rule will sometimes mark the model right and your reference wrong.


**Human review** is ground truth and does not scale. It also drifts, because a reviewer on question 200 is not the reviewer who did question 5. Use it on a stratified sample, with the acceptance criteria written first and two people grading an overlap so you can quote their agreement rate.


**An LLM grader** is the tempting middle, and the honest version is more work than people expect. The MT-Bench paper found strong judges reaching "over 80% agreement" with human preferences, "the same level of agreement between humans", which is the argument for using one. The same paper names position bias, verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias, which are the arguments against trusting one you haven't characterized. The taxonomy's caution on` tsqlet:grading-rule/llm-judged` is one line and it is the whole problem: "Not reproducible across judge models; report the judge and prompt."


Reproducible means: publish the exact prompt, pin the judge model and version, pin temperature at zero, publish per-question verdicts rather than an aggregate, and report the judge's agreement with human review on a sample of a hundred or so items. Without that last number you've replaced a measurement with an opinion that scales.


Never let the grader be the model that wrote the SQL. Panickssery, Bowman and Feng found LLM evaluators recognize their own outputs at "non-trivial accuracy" without special training, score those outputs higher while human annotators rate them equal, and that the bias strength tracks self-recognition ability linearly. Beacon handles it by exclusion: its LLM judge "serves narrative and rubric graders only — never the SQL path."


## A Worked Example You Can Run Today


mnemiq is our open-source text-to-SQL engine, so this section is first-party and the pipeline is readable in the repo. It is here because it ships the three things this method needs and most systems don't expose: an open grader, a tracker holding every run, and per-question results.


Start with the demo, which needs no database of your own and no Docker. The seed step writes a small SQLite database plus its source manifest and access policy under` demo/` .


shell


```text
uv     sync
uv     run     python     scripts  /  seed_demo  .  py


export     MNEMIQ_LLM_BASE_URL  =...    MNEMIQ_LLM_API_KEY  =...    MNEMIQ_LLM_MODEL  =...
export     MNEMIQ_SOURCES_PATH  =  demo  /  sources  .  json
export     MNEMIQ_AUTHZ_PATH  =  demo  /  authz  .  json
export     MNEMIQ_STORE_PATH  =  demo  /  store  .  duckdb


uv     run     mnemiq     enrich          # profile + describe the schema
uv     run     mnemiq     build           # index it for retrieval
uv     run     mnemiq     ask     "how many customers are there by country?"   --  roles     analyst
```


` --roles analyst` is not optional. Access is fail-closed, so without a role the engine grants nothing and defers, which the README notes is "the first thing people mistake for a bug". Two more questions show the parts that aren't the model:


shell


```text
uv     run     mnemiq     ask     "how many enterprise customers are there?"   --  roles     analyst
uv     run     mnemiq     ask     "what was our total revenue last quarter?"     --  roles     analyst
```


The first has to join through a lookup table to resolve a coded column, because` segment_cd` holds` A` /` B` /` C` and nothing in the name says "enterprise". The second is refused: the demo schema has no revenue column, and the engine says so instead of returning a number. Definition band and should-refuse band, in two commands.


Your own question set is a JSON file of cases, in the shape of the shipped` evals/acme.json` :


json


```text
[
{  "id"  :   "churn-q1"  ,   "question"  :   "how many enterprise accounts churned last quarter?"  ,
"gold_sql"  :   "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM account a JOIN segment s ON s.cd = a.segment_cd WHERE s.label = 'enterprise' AND a.churned_at >= '2026-07-01'"  ,
"tags"  : [  "aggregate"  ,   "join"  ,   "coded-value"  ,   "needs-definition"  ]}
]
```


That file is the authoring half of therecord template in mnemiq's own field names:` id` is` question_id` ,` tags` carries the` answerability` band, and` gold_sql` is the provenance for the` expected_result` rows. The run half (` role` ,` system_version` ,` configuration` ,` outcome` ,` latency_ms` and` cost` ) is what you record around the harness, because only you know which settings you varied and what a question cost you.


Three more files ship beside it, and they are the only concrete artifacts the repository publishes.[fs_payments_control.json](https://github.com/agenticfabriq/mnemiq/blob/main/evals/fs_payments_control.json) is a question set with a control band, each case carrying an` expected_answer` note stating *why* that number is right.[fs_payments_authz.json](https://github.com/agenticfabriq/mnemiq/blob/main/evals/fs_payments_authz.json) is its access policy: a role mapped to the tables it may read and its PII clearance, which is the template's` role` field made concrete.[trend.json](https://github.com/agenticfabriq/mnemiq/blob/main/evals/trend.json) is what` eval --record` appends, one object per run with` run_at` ,` total` ,` correct` ,` correct_facts` ,` wrong` ,` deferred_wrongly` ,` error` and two accuracies:` accuracy` over got-the-facts and` strict_accuracy` over exact match. That is the two-denominator discipline expressed as a schema, and it is the shape your own trend log should take.


Be clear about what it is not.` trend.json` is a short trend on the repository's own 30-case demo set, not a benchmark result, and its figures should not be quoted as one. The graded per-question results behind the published comparison are not in this repository at all, because run reports are generated rather than committed; for those, go to beacon.


### Before you point this at a real database


Generated SQL executed against production is the part of this exercise that can hurt you, and the checks belong in front of the query, not in the prompt. mnemiq's decider is a reasonable model of what to demand: the query must be read-only, may only reference objects the caller is allowed to see, must compile in the source's own dialect, and must survive an` EXPLAIN` . Fail one and the answer is a refusal with a stated reason instead of a plausible number. Permissions apply *before* schema retrieval, so a forbidden table is never shown to the model, and row and column policy is applied to the query tree rather than requested of it, because asking a model to respect a filter is not a control.


Three things are yours to provide, and no engine setting substitutes for them:


- **A genuinely read-only database role** , one the database will not let write. mnemiq's Oracle notes are candid that its read plane refuses writes but that the guarantee is partly a property of your deployment: a` SELECT` can reach a writing function through a view, since a view resolves references with the view owner's rights, and restricting the caller does not close that. Opening the database read-only does.
- **A statement timeout and a row cap on that role.** mnemiq exposes connection and probe timeouts for Oracle and documents that data queries are *not* bounded by them, so set these database-side and record which limit fired when one does.
- **Verification on, if you want it.** It is off by default, and the project's own issue tracker notes the verifier fails open when its judge is unreachable. Running with it off is fine; not saying so in` configuration` is how you discover later that half your runs had no brake.


Capture latency and cost at this same boundary: wall-clock in-to-out for` latency_ms` , and tokens or currency for` cost` , remembering that a repair or multi-candidate setting bills several model calls per question.


Then grade it. The harness is part of the engine rather than a separate research project, and it reports six outcomes:` CORRECT` (exact result-set match),` CORRECT_FACTS` (right data, different shape),` WRONG` ,` DEFERRED_CORRECTLY` ,` DEFERRED_WRONGLY` ,` ERROR` — the same six values the template's` outcome` field takes. It prints two accuracies from one run, got-the-facts over answerable and exact match over answerable, which is the two-readings discipline enforced in code.


shell


```text
# the golden set, with a regression gate and a recorded trend point
uv     run     mnemiq     eval   --  golden     evals  /  mine  .  json   --  gate   --  record


# enrichment on, then off, with per-case artifacts: question, gold SQL,
# engine SQL, both result sets, outcome
uv     run     python     scripts  /  run_eval  .  py   --  ab   --  report     reports  /


# a fixed failure becomes a permanent case
uv     run     mnemiq     feedback   --  question     "how many enterprise accounts churned last quarter?"   \
--  sql     "SELECT ..."   --  tables     account  ,  segment   --  golden     evals  /  mine  .  json
```


One wrinkle, because it will bite you.` mnemiq eval` reads its golden set through the Postgres adapter whatever the source manifest says, so it wants` MNEMIQ_PG_DSN` and refuses on a SQLite-only deployment. The no-Docker demo is for the ask loop and the refusal behaviour; point the eval at a Postgres slice of your own.


For third-party grading, push the outputs to[beacon](https://github.com/agenticfabriq/beacon) , a tracker and not an executor: you register a run, execute it on your own hardware with your own runner, and push the rows your engine returned. Beacon grades those rows against gold it already holds, so no benchmark database is needed at grading time and the system under test never marks its own homework.` beacon suites create` makes the question set,` beacon eval run` registers the run,` scripts/load_eval_reports.py` loads JSONL reports, and` beacon audit spot-check` re-executes a sample of the pushed SQL on a named engine. Loading a report doubles as a conformance check between two independent graders, and the disagreement table it prints is the reason to bother.


## What Makes a Number Dishonest


Four ways, and all four are easy to do by accident.


**Tuning on the test set.** You run the set, see the definition band fail, add the definitions, rerun, report the new number. Good engineering loop, ruined measurement, because the set is now a training signal.


Text-to-SQL leaks in a way that is easy to miss, because the thing you tune is not a model. Every honest fix you make (a glossary entry, a certified definition, a table description, a few-shot example, a` feedback` case promoted into the golden set) gets written *because* you read a failing question. Enrichment is the worst offender: it makes an LLM pass over the schema and writes descriptions that your current questions can shape, deliberately or not. After that the system is not answering a held-out question, it is answering one whose vocabulary is already in its context.


So split the set before you look at a single result, and keep the held-out slice out of the room:


- Draw it as a stratified sample so every band is represented, not by taking the last ten rows.
- Enrich, build, write definitions and promote feedback cases on the development slice **only** . No held-out question's text, gold SQL or business term goes into a description, glossary, example or prompt.
- Store it where the tuning loop cannot read it, and run it on a schedule rather than whenever a number disappoints.
- Record which slice produced a figure: a development number and a held-out number are different metrics.
- Touch it and it is spent. A held-out question that has driven a fix is a development question for good.


If you have 30 questions and can't afford to hold any out, report the tuned number and label it as tuned.


**Grading with the model that wrote the SQL.** Covered above: self-recognition tracks self-preference, and the bias is measurable. Different family for the judge, or no LLM judge on the SQL path at all.


**Reporting one run.** Eighty unique completions out of a thousand identical temperature-zero requests is what the floor looks like. A single run has no error bar and you can't add one afterwards.


**Quoting a public benchmark number as yours.** A BIRD score is a statement about databases somebody else curated. Repeating it in a slide about your warehouse is the move this method exists to replace, and it is the subject of the companion piece on[why BIRD and Spider rankings disagree](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/blog/why-bird-and-spider-rankings-disagree) .


Vendor accuracy claims have the same problem one level up: two managed systems quoting different numbers on different data are not comparable until somebody runs them on the same questions. That exercise is[Cortex Analyst vs Databricks Genie on accuracy](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/blog/cortex-analyst-vs-genie-accuracy) .


A fifth, quieter one: changing the grader and comparing across the change. Beacon's re-basing note is the honest version. Spider EX quoted before 2026-08-07 was 53.4% on a local slice under the runner's pre-convergence grading, and 55.7% on the same run once EX derived from beacon's verdicts. Their rule is that comparisons across that boundary must re-base, with the run config and dataset version distinguishing the two eras. Change the grader and every earlier number is a different metric.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**How do I evaluate text-to-SQL on my own database?** Build 20 to 30 real questions from your BI query log, tag each as answerable from column names, needs a definition, or should be refused, write reference answers by running a human-written gold query and storing its rows, fix the grading rule and the denominators in writing before you look at any output, hold a slice back, run the full set at least three times under one recorded configuration, and report right, refused and wrong separately plus the case-flip rate.


**Is the SQL graded, or the result?** The result. Execute both the candidate query and the reference query and compare the rows that come back; never compare the SQL text. Two queries sharing no tokens can be equally correct, so string-matching marks correct answers wrong. Keep the generated SQL beside the verdict as evidence to read, not as the thing scored.


**How many questions do I need?** Twenty to thirty to diagnose which layer is broken. Several hundred to rank two configurations: Miller's worked example puts a three-point difference at 80% power and 5% significance at roughly 969 paired questions.


**Should I use exact match or result containment?** Both, side by side, with the gap between them named. Exact match is leaderboard-comparable and produces false negatives: the test-suite accuracy paper measured 2.5% average and 8.1% worst-case false negatives for Spider's own metric across 21 submissions. Result containment matches what an analyst accepts.


**Can I use an LLM to grade text-to-SQL?** For narrative or rubric answers, with the prompt published, the judge model and version pinned, temperature at zero, per-question verdicts published and an agreement rate against human review on a sample. Not for comparing result sets, where deterministic comparison is cheaper and reproducible, and never using the model that generated the SQL.


**How many runs should I do?** Three minimum, with mean and spread both reported. Temperature zero does not make a run reproducible: 1,000 identical requests to Qwen3-235B at temperature 0 produced 80 unique completions.


**Do refusals count as wrong answers?** Not as wrong, but they cannot vanish either. Report accuracy twice: over the questions the system answered, and over every gradeable question in the set, which keeps refusals in the denominator. The first rises as a system refuses more; the second falls. Report the deferral rate, over-refusals and the refusal hold beside them. Errors leave the accuracy denominator and get their own count, split by cause.


**What is a good text-to-SQL accuracy number?** There isn't one. The number is a joint property of your schema, your question mix and your grading rule. What you can compare is one question set under two configurations of the same system, and that comparison tells you what to build next.


**How do I know if the evaluation itself is wrong?** Have a second grader re-grade the same stored rows and read the disagreements. Beacon's report loader prints exactly that table.


## Conclusion


The number you want is not hard to compute. It is hard to make honest, and almost all of that difficulty sits in decisions made before any SQL is generated: which questions, written by whom, stratified how, graded under which rule, averaged over how many runs, with refusals counted where.


For the renewals slice at that B2B company, a defensible first result is twenty-eight questions from the BI log in three bands, a held-out third, reference rows written by the analytics lead, both grading rules reported, three runs under one recorded configuration, and five numbers rather than one: band accuracy, deferral rate, over-refusals, errors by cause, case-flip rate. That takes an afternoon and tells you whether to spend the next quarter writing a glossary or tuning retrieval. A BIRD score tells you neither.


**The test we'd apply before quoting any text-to-SQL number:** name the question set, the grading rule, the run count and the refusal policy in one sentence. If you can't, you have a percentage rather than a measurement, and the two are not interchangeable.
